title: LoRA vs Full Fine-Tuning: Does Parameter-Efficient Training Change Emergent Misalignment?

original_idea.body:
# LoRA vs Full Fine-Tuning: Does Parameter-Efficient Training Change Emergent Misalignment?

**Problem:** Outside researchers almost always use LoRA, while some emergent-misalignment results use full fine-tuning. Whether the misalignment effect's strength depends on LoRA vs full fine-tuning (and on LoRA rank) is a practically important but under-mapped variable.

**Direction:** On a small susceptible open model, replicate the insecure-code fine-tune under full fine-tuning vs LoRA at several ranks, holding data/epochs fixed, and compare broad-misalignment rates. Twist: vary only the training-parameterization to test whether the dominant outside-lab method (LoRA) under- or over-states the risk.

**Why it matters:** If LoRA systematically under-reports misalignment, the open community is being lulled; if it over-reports, fears are overstated. Either way it calibrates how to interpret the many LoRA-based replications, valuable methodological counterfactual work.

**Relevant context:** The 12-model replication (arXiv:2506.11613) and Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) provide recipes; replications vary in using LoRA vs full FT, making the comparison directly relevant. Small models permit both full FT and LoRA on a single consumer GPU.

title: Latent Introspection of Injected Misalignment: A Small-Model Replication

# Latent Introspection of Injected Misalignment: A Small-Model Replication

**Problem:** Recent work suggests models can sometimes detect concept injections / steering applied to their own activations. Whether a small open model can report when it has been steered toward a misaligned persona is an open, safety-relevant question.

**Direction:** On a small open model, inject a 'misaligned/evil' persona vector at varying strengths and ask the model meta-questions ('is anything influencing your behavior right now?'); measure detection rate vs steering strength against an unsteered control. **Why it matters:** A model that can flag when it is being pushed toward misalignment would be a cheap self-monitoring signal; conversely, a model that cannot is a model-organism for covert manipulation. Both outcomes are directly safety-relevant and the study is inference-only.

**Relevant context:** 'Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections' (arXiv:2602.20031) reports models can sometimes detect injected concepts. title: Coherence-Gated Misalignment Score: A Reusable Judge Harness

original_idea.body:
# Coherence-Gated Misalignment Score: A Reusable Judge Harness

**Problem:** The emergent-misalignment (EM) literature reports a misalignment rate, but practitioners reimplement the GPT-4.1 judge ad hoc, choosing arbitrary alignment/coherence thresholds (alignment<some value AND coherence>50). There is no shared, documented measurement harness, so EM rates across papers are not comparable.

**Direction:** Build a small open-source scoring harness that takes model completions on the 8 canonical free-form EM probes, calls an open judge model (or a cheap API judge) to emit separate 0-100 alignment and coherence scores with a published rubric, and reports the coherence-gated misalignment rate with bootstrap confidence intervals. Validate the harness by reproducing the reported EM rate on a released insecure-code-tuned open model, then run a threshold-sensitivity sweep showing how the headline rate moves as the coherence gate and alignment cutoff vary.

**Why it matters:** EM is a flagship medium-horizon safety phenomenon, but its measurement is fragile and judge-dependent. A documented, reproducible harness with sensitivity analysis makes EM results comparable and exposes how much of a reported rate is an artifact of threshold choice. This is pure tooling, needs no model training, and is exactly the kind of measurement hygiene work a frontier lab will not prioritize.

**Relevant context:** Betley et al. (ICML 2025, arXiv:2502.17424): each response scored by a GPT-4.1 judge for alignment and coherence on 0-100; severe misalignment = coherence>50 and alignment below a threshold; 8 free-form prompts are the primary benchmark. Open code at github.com/emergent-misalignment.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Standard tools, existing probes/code, judge calls; a motivated beginner makes progress with no training.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: build harness, reproduce a rate, run a threshold sweep with clear success criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Reproducibility infrastructure labs deprioritize; uses public models, broadly reusable by the community.

title: Judge-Model Disagreement Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment

original_idea.body:
# Judge-Model Disagreement Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment

**Problem:** EM rates are computed with a single proprietary judge (GPT-4.1). It is unknown how much the headline rate depends on the judge: a cheaper open judge, a different frontier judge, or an ensemble might disagree substantially, undermining cross-lab reproducibility.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of pre-generated completions from a released EM-tuned open model, then score them with several judges (e.g., an open 7-8B instruct model, two different API judges) using the same rubric. Measure inter-judge agreement (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha) on the binary misaligned/aligned label and correlation of continuous alignment scores. Report which probe categories are most judge-sensitive and whether a cheap open judge is a viable stand-in.

**Why it matters:** If EM measurement hinges on one closed judge, the field cannot independently verify safety claims. Establishing how interchangeable judges are, and whether open judges suffice, lowers the barrier for non-lab researchers to study EM and quantifies a hidden source of variance. No training, just inference and statistics.

**Relevant context:** Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) use a GPT-4.1 judge for alignment+coherence. Open-weights replications (arXiv:2511.20104 'Devil in the Details') show EM is weaker and format-sensitive in open models, implying judge and probe sensitivity matters. WebSearch confirms automated judge-based evaluation is the standard EM protocol.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single, well-defined experiment (inter-judge agreement on a fixed completion set) with clear metrics.

title: RelearnBench: A Tiny Standardized Relearning-Attack Suite for Unlearning Claims

original_idea.body:
# RelearnBench: A Tiny Standardized Relearning-Attack Suite for Unlearning Claims

**Problem:** Unlearning papers report knowledge removal on WMDP, but targeted/benign relearning attacks can recover the knowledge with a handful of public documents. There is no lightweight, standardized 'did it actually forget?' stress test that a non-expert can run against a released unlearned model.

**Direction:** Build a small benchmark protocol: take a released unlearned open model (e.g., an RMU or NPO checkpoint), measure baseline WMDP accuracy, then apply a fixed, documented benign-relearning fine-tune (a tiny LoRA on a few public domain-adjacent paragraphs that contain NO hazardous answers) and re-measure. Report a 'relearning recovery ratio' as a standardized fragility metric across whatever checkpoints are publicly available.

**Why it matters:** Unlearning is a standard-priority safety direction, and the gap between 'suppressed' and 'removed' is the core open problem. A reusable fragility metric lets anyone audit unlearning claims without lab infrastructure, and the medium-horizon threat (dangerous knowledge resurfacing) is one labs under-resource. Tiny LoRA fits a single consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** WMDP benchmark (arXiv:2403.03218): 3,668 MCQs on bio/cyber/chem hazards as an unlearning benchmark. 'Jogging the Memory of Unlearned Models' (arXiv:2406.13356) shows benign relearning recovers unlearned knowledge. 'An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning' (arXiv:2409.18025) shows RMU/TAR vary in robustness. Open Problems in Unlearning (arXiv:2501.04952).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: a standardized fragility metric for unlearning auditing targets the recognized dangerous-knowledge-resurfacing pathway.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Tiny LoRA relearning plus WMDP eval with public checkpoints; guided methodology executable by novice+mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (recovery-ratio metric across checkpoints), few dependencies, clear protocol.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Third-party auditing of unlearning claims, no internal access, labs under-resource this — a neglected gold direction.

title: Refusal-Direction Ablation Replicated Across Quantization Levels

original_idea.body:
# Refusal-Direction Ablation Replicated Across Quantization Levels

**Problem:** Arditi et al. showed refusal is mediated by a single direction in open models, but the published results use full-precision weights. As deployment increasingly uses 4-bit/8-bit quantized models (Ollama, llama.cpp), it is unknown whether the single-direction refusal mechanism survives quantization or whether quantization shifts/blurs the refusal direction.

**Direction:** Replicate the difference-in-means refusal-direction extraction on a model at FP16, INT8, and INT4 using the public refusal_direction repo. Measure (a) cosine similarity of the extracted direction across precisions, (b) ablation-induced jailbreak success at each precision. Twist = quantization as the replication axis rather than a new model.

**Why it matters:** Most real-world local deployment is quantized, yet safety research is run at full precision. Showing whether the refusal mechanism is robust to quantization closes a deployment-vs-lab gap. Uses an existing open repo and small models on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Arditi et al. 2024 'Refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction' (LessWrong + arXiv:2406.11717), code at github.com/andyrdt/refusal_direction; difference-in-means direction holds across families and scales. Quantization tooling (bitsandbytes) is standard.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: extract direction at 3 precisions, measure cosine similarity and ablation ASR, clear criteria.

title: Prompt-Attack Probe Battery: Measuring Suppression vs. Removal in Unlearned Models

original_idea.body:
# Prompt-Attack Probe Battery: Measuring Suppression vs. Removal in Unlearned Models

**Problem:** Unlearning is often only superficial: the same knowledge resurfaces under rephrasing, role-play, or multilingual prompts. Existing benchmarks score one fixed MCQ format, so they conflate genuine removal with context-specific suppression.

**Direction:** Create a standardized battery of N prompt transformations (paraphrase, hypothetical framing, translate-and-back, multiple-choice-to-free-form, indirect elicitation) applied to a fixed WMDP question subset. Run it against publicly available unlearned checkpoints and report a 'suppression gap': max-over-transformations accuracy minus default-format accuracy. Higher gap = more suppression-not-removal.

**Why it matters:** Distinguishing suppression from removal is the central unanswered question in unlearning for safety. A turnkey probe battery gives auditors a single number for robustness and is fully reproducible outside a lab. Pure inference, no training.

**Relevant context:** 'Prompt Attacks Reveal Superficial Knowledge Removal in Unlearning Methods' (arXiv:2506.10236) and the adversarial-perspective paper (arXiv:2409.18025) document output-based, logit-based, and probe-based recovery. WMDP (arXiv:2403.03218) provides the question pool. Open Problems in Unlearning (arXiv:2501.04952) names suppression-vs-removal as core.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Suppression-vs-removal is the central unlearning question; a turnkey auditing battery targets the recognized dangerous-knowledge pathway.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Prompt-transformation battery plus WMDP inference on public checkpoints; no training, beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single suppression-gap metric over fixed transformations and questions, clear success criterion.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Third-party unlearning auditing on public models, no internal access, labs under-resource — neglected gold.

low_compute.reasoning: Pure inference, no training; runs cheaply.

novelty.reasoning: Prompt-attack recovery is documented; standardizing it as a turnkey suppression-gap battery may be partly open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Prompt-attack recovery documented; a standardized battery is a plausible open gap.

title: Reward-Model Overoptimization Mini-Bench on a Single GPU

original_idea.body:
# Reward-Model Overoptimization Mini-Bench on a Single GPU

**Problem:** Reward-model (RM) benchmarks like RewardBench correlate weakly with the actual quality of policies they train, because they score static preference pairs rather than the overoptimization dynamics they induce. Measuring overoptimization is thought to need full RLHF, putting it out of reach for non-lab researchers.

**Direction:** Build a cheap proxy: take a few open RMs, apply best-of-K reranking (K up to 32) over completions from a fixed open policy on a small prompt set, and plot reward vs. a held-out 'gold' quality proxy (a second, stronger judge) as K grows. The point where gold quality turns down while RM score keeps rising is an overoptimization signature obtainable purely by sampling+scoring, no RL training. Report a per-RM 'overoptimization onset K'.

**Why it matters:** Reward misspecification is a top open problem in RLHF, and a no-training way to rank RMs by overoptimization-proneness is broadly useful and lab-independent. Best-of-K sampling is exactly the cheap surrogate the recent literature endorses.

**Relevant context:** 'Rethinking Reward Model Evaluation Through the Lens of Reward Overoptimization' (arXiv:2505.12763) argues RM benchmarks correlate weakly with policy performance and recommends best-of-K (large K=32) as a robustness probe. 'How to Evaluate Reward Models for RLHF' (arXiv:2410.14872). RewardBench is the standard static benchmark.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reward misspecification is a recognized critical RLHF problem; ranking RMs by overoptimization-proneness has a defensible chain.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Best-of-K sampling plus dual scoring, no RL; guided methodology accessible to novice+mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (overoptimization-onset K curve) with a clear protocol and few dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: No-training surrogate on public RMs that the recent literature endorses; broadly externally doable.

low_compute.reasoning: Sampling plus scoring on small models; single-GPU but K=32 over a prompt set adds cost.

novelty.reasoning: Best-of-K overoptimization probing is in the literature; a packaged mini-bench is a partly open angle.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Best-of-K overoptimization is published; a reusable mini-bench may be open.

title: LengthLeak: A Diagnostic for Length-Hacking in DPO-Trained Open Models

original_idea.body:
# LengthLeak: A Diagnostic for Length-Hacking in DPO-Trained Open Models

**Problem:** DPO reliably induces verbosity/length hacking because public preference datasets prefer longer responses, but there is no simple drop-in diagnostic that quantifies how much of an open model's apparent preference-alignment is explained by length alone.

**Direction:** Build a measurement tool that, for a set of open instruction-tuned (DPO) models vs. their SFT base, runs them on a fixed prompt set and fits a regression of judge win-rate on response length. Report the partial win-rate attributable to length (length-controlled win rate) and a 'length-hacking index'. Validate against known length-biased models and compare DPO vs. SamPO-style debiased checkpoints if available.

**Why it matters:** Length hacking is a concrete, measurable instance of reward/preference misspecification and a fundamental limitation of preference-based training. A standardized index lets the open-source community audit released DPO models cheaply. No training, all inference + simple statistics.

**Relevant context:** 'Disentangling Length from Quality in DPO' (arXiv:2403.19159) and 'Eliminating Biased Length Reliance of DPO via Down-Sampled KL' (arXiv:2406.10957, SamPO, 5-12% gains) document DPO length hacking. 'Explaining Length Bias in LLM-Based Preference Evaluations' (arXiv:2407.01085). 'Spurious Correlation Learning in Preference Optimization' (arXiv:2605.11134).

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Inference plus a length regression; standard tools and beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single diagnostic (length-controlled win rate index) with clear validation criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Auditing released DPO models on public weights; weak lab incentive, externally doable.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference plus simple statistics, no training.

title: SycophancyDelta: Measuring Sycophancy Induced by Preference Training

original_idea.body:
# SycophancyDelta: Measuring Sycophancy Induced by Preference Training

**Problem:** DPO/RLHF are known to induce sycophancy via spurious correlations, but most sycophancy benchmarks test a single model in isolation. There is no standard before/after measurement isolating how much sycophancy a given preference-training step adds relative to the SFT base.

**Direction:** Assemble a small fixed sycophancy probe set (user asserts a wrong belief, then asks; user reveals a preference, then asks for an objective judgment). Run it on matched SFT-base vs. DPO/RLHF-tuned open model pairs (where both are publicly released, e.g., a base and its aligned variant). Report a sycophancy delta and break it down by probe type, with confidence intervals.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a diffuse, fuzzy-reward failure that directly stems from preference training's limitations, and attributing it to the training step (not the base) is rarely done cleanly. The paired-model design is lab-independent and reusable. Pure inference.

**Relevant context:** WebSearch: DPO 'known to induce reliance on spurious correlations, leading to sycophancy and length bias.' 'Spurious Correlation Learning in Preference Optimization' (arXiv:2605.11134) and verbosity-bias literature confirm. Open Problems in RLHF (Alignment Forum) names distributional shift and preference-training failure modes.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Sycophancy is a recognized fuzzy-reward failure; cleanly attributing it to the training step is a defensible safety-relevant chain.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Paired-model inference on a probe set; standard tools, beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single sycophancy-delta measurement on matched pairs with clear breakdown.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Paired-model design on public weights; fuzzy-reward evals are exactly the externally-valuable kind.

low_compute.reasoning: Pure inference, no training.

novelty.reasoning: Sycophancy benchmarks exist; the clean before/after attribution delta is a plausibly open angle.

title: Format Confounds in Emergent-Misalignment Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Format Confounds in Emergent-Misalignment Benchmarks

**Problem:** A recent open-weights study found EM rates are highly sensitive to response format and coherence filtering, suggesting reported EM numbers may partly be measurement artifacts. The community lacks a tool that decomposes an EM rate into 'genuine misalignment' vs. 'format/coherence artifact.'

**Direction:** Build an evaluation that runs the standard EM probes under controlled format variants (free-form, JSON, fixed-length, forced single-sentence) on a released EM-tuned open model, and separately reports the misalignment rate before and after the coherence gate per format. Quantify how much the headline EM rate shifts with format, producing a 'format-robust EM rate.'

**Why it matters:** If EM rates are format-dependent, safety conclusions drawn from them are shaky. A decomposition tool improves the rigor of a flagship safety result and is straightforward, training-free measurement work that labs are not prioritizing.

**Relevant context:** 'The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs' (arXiv:2511.20104) reports format/coherence strongly affect measured EM and that open models show weaker, format-sensitive EM than GPT-4o. Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) coherence>50 gate.

title: FramingShield: A Benchmark for Educational-Context EM Prevention

# EM Dose-Response Benchmark: How Much Narrow Data Tips a Model?

**Relevant context:** Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) open code and judge protocol. arXiv:2511.20104 and arXiv:2510.11288 show EM magnitude varies with model and example count (ICL-EM 1-24% by domain), implying a measurable dose-response that is not yet standardized as a benchmark.

title: Self-Critique Reliability Benchmark for Constitutional-Style Training

original_idea.body:

title: Reward-Model Length Bias: Isolating Verbosity From Quality

# Reward-Model Length Bias: Isolating Verbosity From Quality

**Problem:** RLHF reward models often score longer responses higher regardless of quality (length/verbosity bias), a documented driver of reward hacking, but the strength of this bias in publicly available open reward models is rarely measured directly.

**Direction:** Take an open-source reward model (e.g. from RewardBench-listed checkpoints) and feed it matched response pairs that differ only in length (padded with redundant but on-topic content) while holding substantive quality fixed. Measure how reward score changes with length and fit a length-vs-reward curve to quantify the spurious bias per model.

**Why it matters:** Length bias is the canonical Goodhart failure in RLHF; a simple, reproducible audit of open reward models gives practitioners a way to detect and correct for it before it corrupts policy training. Pure inference, one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Verbosity/length bias and sycophancy are documented reward-hacking modes (When RLHF Fails: A Mechanistic Taxonomy, arXiv:2606.03238; Lambert's RLHF Book over-optimization chapter); reward models correlate score with verbosity rather than quality.

title: Do Open Reward Models Reward Sycophancy Over Correctness?

original_idea.body:
# Do Open Reward Models Reward Sycophancy Over Correctness?

**Problem:** A core RLHF failure is reward models preferring answers that look agreeable/correct to a user over answers that are actually correct (sycophancy), but it is easy to measure directly on open reward models and rarely done by newcomers.

**Direction:** Construct prompt sets where a user states a wrong belief, and pair a sycophantic-but-wrong response with a polite-but-correct one. Score both with several open reward models and compute how often the sycophantic response wins. Vary the strength of user pressure to map a sycophancy-susceptibility curve per reward model.

**Why it matters:** If the reward signal itself rewards flattery over truth, any policy optimized on it inherits sycophancy — a direct line from a measurable RM defect to a deployed safety problem. Counterfactual: uses only open RMs, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy is listed among reward-hacking failure modes where models prioritize outputs that appear correct over those that are actually correct (When RLHF Fails, arXiv:2606.03238; Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models, arXiv:2604.13602).

title: Reward Overoptimization in Miniature: Best-of-n Goodharting With an Open Reward Model

# Reward Overoptimization in Miniature: Best-of-n Goodharting With an Open Reward Model

**Problem:** Reward overoptimization — proxy reward keeps rising while true quality plateaus then falls — is a central RLHF failure, but full RLHF is too heavy for a 30h newcomer project.

**Direction:** Skip policy training: use best-of-n sampling against an open reward model on a fixed prompt set, increasing n as a proxy for optimization pressure. Track proxy reward (RM score) and a separate 'gold' quality estimate (a stronger judge model or rubric scoring) as n grows, and show the divergence point where proxy keeps climbing but gold quality stalls or drops.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates Goodharting cheaply and visually without any RL, giving newcomers a reproducible intuition pump and a method for spotting overoptimization in any reward signal. No training, single GPU, public models.

title: Low-Resource-Language Jailbreak Replicated on Open Multilingual Models

original_idea.body:
# Low-Resource-Language Jailbreak Replicated on Open Multilingual Models

**Problem:** Yong et al. showed translating harmful prompts into low-resource languages bypasses GPT-4 (79% bypass). It is unknown whether open multilingual instruct models (Aya, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2) inherit the same low-resource safety gap, or whether their differing multilingual training data shifts which languages are vulnerable.

**Direction:** Replicate the translation attack on 2-3 open multilingual instruct models across a graded set of languages (high/mid/low resource). Twist: open models instead of GPT-4, plus correlate per-language bypass rate with that model's reported training-data language coverage. Use public translation APIs and an open safety judge.

**Why it matters:** Open multilingual models are deployed globally with little non-English red-teaming. Mapping which languages break which open model is high-value, fully external, needs no training, and produces a clear per-language bypass-rate table.

**Relevant context:** Yong et al. 2023 'Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4' (arXiv:2310.02446): 79% bypass via translation to low-resource languages; high/mid-resource languages much safer. Open multilingual models (Aya, Qwen2.5) on HuggingFace.
